# One-Dimensional Scattering for a PT-Symmetric Potential

## Problem Setup

In this work, we consider a one-dimensional scattering problem for a complex, PT-symmetric short-range potential V(x). PT-symmetry refers to the invariance of the system under the combined operations of parity (P) and time reversal (T). Such potentials have attracted considerable attention because, despite being non-Hermitian, they can exhibit entirely real energy spectra and physically meaningful scattering behavior, provided the PT-symmetry remains unbroken. The short-range character of the potential ensures that it vanishes sufficiently rapidly at large distances, allowing for the standard definition of asymptotic scattering states.

## Analytical Framework

The central object of our analysis is the time-independent Schrödinger equation governing the scattering process. To handle the complex nature of the potential and to obtain quantitatively reliable results, we employ a Runge-Kutta-discretized version of this equation. By discretizing the spatial domain and propagating the wavefunction numerically according to the Runge-Kutta scheme, we are able to accurately capture the evolution of the scattering states across the region where the potential is non-negligible. This approach provides a robust and flexible foundation for treating potentials whose complexity would render purely analytical methods intractable.

## Derivation of Scattering Coefficients

From this discretized formulation, we derive explicit formulae for the reflection and transmission coefficients. These coefficients characterize the fundamental outcomes of the scattering event: the reflection coefficient quantifies the fraction of the incident wave that is reflected back by the potential, while the transmission coefficient describes the portion that passes through. By matching the numerically propagated wavefunction to the asymptotic plane-wave solutions on either side of the potential, we obtain expressions for both quantities directly in terms of the discretized quantities computed along the spatial grid.

## Key Innovation

The principal innovation of this approach lies in the complexification of one of the parameters that characterizes the potential. By allowing this parameter to take complex values, we introduce the non-Hermitian, PT-symmetric structure into the problem in a controlled and systematic manner. This complexification is the essential mechanism through which the distinctive features of PT-symmetric scattering—such as anomalous reflection and transmission behavior—emerge, and it constitutes the core methodological contribution of the present study.

# One-Dimensional Scattering from a PT-Symmetric Short-Range Potential

## Introduction

The study of quantum scattering in one dimension provides one of the most transparent settings in which to explore the consequences of non-Hermitian, parity-time (PT) symmetric potentials. While conventional quantum mechanics restricts the Hamiltonian to be Hermitian in order to guarantee real energy eigenvalues and a unitary evolution, the discovery that PT-symmetric potentials can also possess entirely real spectra has opened a rich field of inquiry. In this work, we investigate the one-dimensional scattering problem for a complex, PT-symmetric short-range potential, with the aim of deriving explicit formulae for the reflection and transmission coefficients.

## Method

Our approach is based on a Runge-Kutta-discretized version of the time-independent Schrödinger equation. Rather than seeking closed-form analytic solutions—which are available only for a restricted class of potentials—we recast the second-order differential equation as a system of first-order equations suitable for numerical integration. The Runge-Kutta scheme allows the wavefunction and its derivative to be propagated across the region of nonvanishing potential, from which the scattering behavior can be extracted.

Because the potential is short-range, the wavefunction reduces to a superposition of incoming and outgoing plane waves in the asymptotic regions on either side of the interaction zone. By matching the numerically propagated solution to these asymptotic forms, we obtain expressions for the reflection coefficient $R$ and the transmission coefficient $T$. This discretized framework has the advantage of being applicable to essentially arbitrary potential profiles, while still reproducing the standard results in the appropriate limits.

## Results and Discussion

The central finding of our analysis is both simple and instructive: the entire effect of imposing PT symmetry on the potential can be traced to the complexification of a single parameter among those that characterize the potential. In the Hermitian case, this parameter takes real values, and the resulting reflection and transmission coefficients obey the familiar constraints, including the conservation of probability flux, $R + T = 1$.

When PT symmetry is introduced, the potential acquires a complex structure satisfying $V(x) = V^*(-x)$, meaning its real part is even and its imaginary part is odd in the spatial coordinate. Remarkably, within our formulation this modification manifests solely through allowing one of the potential-characterizing parameters to become complex. All of the algebraic machinery developed for the Hermitian problem carries over unchanged; only the analytic continuation of this parameter into the complex plane is required.

This observation has significant conceptual value. It demonstrates that PT-symmetric scattering need not be treated as an entirely separate theoretical construct, but can instead be incorporated into the standard scattering framework with minimal modification. Consequences characteristic of non-Hermitian systems—such as the possible violation of the unitarity relation $R + T = 1$, the emergence of anomalous transmission, and the phenomenon of unidirectional invisibility—all follow naturally once the relevant parameter is complexified.

## Conclusion

We have shown that the one-dimensional scattering problem for a complex, PT-symmetric short-range potential can be efficiently treated using a Runge-Kutta-discretized Schrödinger equation, yielding compact formulae for the reflection and transmission coefficients. The key insight is that the transition from a Hermitian to a PT-symmetric description requires only the complexification of one parameter, underscoring the economy with which PT symmetry can be embedded in conventional scattering theory. This result not only simplifies the analysis of such systems but also clarifies the essential mathematical origin of their distinctive physical behavior.

# Solving Differential Equations Using the Runge-Kutta Method

## Introduction

One of the most powerful and widely used techniques for numerically solving ordinary differential equations (ODEs) is the Runge-Kutta method. Developed by German mathematicians Carl Runge and Wilhelm Kutta around the turn of the 20th century, this family of iterative methods has become a cornerstone of computational mathematics, engineering, and the physical sciences.

## Why Use Runge-Kutta?

When faced with a differential equation that cannot be solved analytically, one must turn to numerical approximation. While simpler approaches like Euler's method exist, they often lack the accuracy needed for practical applications. Using the Runge-Kutta method offers a significant improvement in precision without requiring the computation of higher-order derivatives, making it both efficient and reliable.

## The Fourth-Order Method

The most popular variant is the classical fourth-order Runge-Kutta method (often abbreviated as RK4). Using this approach, one estimates the solution at each step by combining four separate calculations:

- **k₁** — the slope at the beginning of the interval
- **k₂** — the slope at the midpoint, using k₁
- **k₃** — a refined slope at the midpoint, using k₂
- **k₄** — the slope at the end of the interval

These values are then combined in a weighted average to produce the next point in the solution. One key advantage of this technique is that it balances computational cost with accuracy remarkably well.

## Practical Applications

Using the Runge-Kutta method, scientists and engineers can model a vast range of dynamic systems, including:

- Planetary and satellite orbits
- Population growth models
- Chemical reaction kinetics
- Electrical circuit behavior
- Fluid dynamics simulations

## Conclusion

The Runge-Kutta method remains one of the most trusted tools in numerical analysis. By using it, one gains a practical means of approximating solutions to complex problems that would otherwise be impossible to solve by hand, demonstrating the enduring value of the work pioneered by Runge and Kutta over a century ago.

The stationary Schrödinger equation is recast as a system of coupled first-order ordinary differential equations and integrated using a fourth-order Runge-Kutta scheme, with transmission and reflection coefficients extracted by matching the numerical solution to asymptotic plane-wave boundary conditions. We systematically explore the dependence of the scattering observables on the incident particle energy and on the relative strength of the gain-loss parameter V₂. Our results reveal the hallmark features of PT-symmetric scattering, including asymmetric (handedness-dependent) reflection—wherein reflection from the left and right differ—while transmission remains reciprocal. As V₂ is increased toward the exceptional point associated with spontaneous PT-symmetry breaking, we observe the emergence of anomalous transport regimes characterized by reflectionless transmission and the onset of unidirectional invisibility. Convergence studies confirm the numerical stability and accuracy of the Runge-Kutta integration across the parameter space examined. These findings illustrate the rich phenomenology of non-Hermitian scattering and demonstrate the efficacy of direct numerical integration as a versatile tool for probing complex-potential systems relevant to optical waveguides, metamaterials, and open quantum systems.

counterfactuals.output:
# Runge-Kutta Discretization of the Schrödinger Equation for Scattering Coefficients in Complex Potentials

## Abstract

This summary describes the numerical framework by which a Runge-Kutta (RK) integration scheme applied to the time-independent Schrödinger equation yields expressions for the reflection and transmission coefficients associated with scattering from a complex (non-Hermitian) potential. The treatment emphasizes the connection between the numerically propagated wavefunction and the asymptotic boundary conditions that define the scattering amplitudes.

## Governing Equation

Consider the one-dimensional stationary Schrödinger equation for a particle of mass $m$ and energy $E$,

$$
-\frac{\hbar^2}{2m}\frac{d^2\psi(x)}{dx^2} + V(x)\,\psi(x) = E\,\psi(x),
$$

where the potential is permitted to be complex, $V(x) = V_R(x) + i\,V_I(x)$. The imaginary component $V_I(x)$ accounts for absorptive or emissive processes and renders the associated Hamiltonian non-Hermitian, so that probability current is not conserved and $R + T \neq 1$ in general.

It is convenient to define $k^2(x) = \tfrac{2m}{\hbar^2}\,[E - V(x)]$, giving

$$
\psi''(x) + k^2(x)\,\psi(x) = 0.
$$

## Reduction to a First-Order System

To apply a Runge-Kutta scheme, the second-order equation is recast as a coupled first-order system. Introducing the auxiliary variable $\phi(x) = \psi'(x)$, one obtains

$$
\frac{d}{dx}
\begin{pmatrix} \psi \\ \phi \end{pmatrix}
=
\begin{pmatrix} 0 & 1 \\ -k^2(x) & 0 \end{pmatrix}
\begin{pmatrix} \psi \\ \phi \end{pmatrix}
\equiv \mathbf{F}(x,\mathbf{y}).
$$

Because $k^2(x)$ is complex, both $\psi$ and $\phi$ are complex-valued, and the integration is carried out in the complex plane.

## Runge-Kutta Propagation

A standard fourth-order Runge-Kutta (RK4) update advances the solution vector $\mathbf{y}_n = \mathbf{y}(x_n)$ over a step of size $h$ according to

$$
\mathbf{y}_{n+1} = \mathbf{y}_n + \frac{h}{6}\left(\mathbf{k}_1 + 2\mathbf{k}_2 + 2\mathbf{k}_3 + \mathbf{k}_4\right),
$$

with the stage derivatives

$$
\begin{aligned}
\mathbf{k}_1 &= \mathbf{F}(x_n,\mathbf{y}_n), \\
\mathbf{k}_2 &= \mathbf{F}\!\left(x_n+\tfrac{h}{2},\,\mathbf{y}_n+\tfrac{h}{2}\mathbf{k}_1\right), \\
\mathbf{k}_3 &= \mathbf{F}\!\left(x_n+\tfrac{h}{2},\,\mathbf{y}_n+\tfrac{h}{2}\mathbf{k}_2\right), \\
\mathbf{k}_4 &= \mathbf{F}\!\left(x_n+h,\,\mathbf{y}_n+h\,\mathbf{k}_3\right).
\end{aligned}
$$

The linearity of $\mathbf{F}$ ensures that the RK4 map is itself linear in $\mathbf{y}$, so propagation across the interaction region $[x_L, x_R]$ is equivalent to multiplication by a transfer matrix $\mathbf{M}$,

$$
\mathbf{y}(x_R) = \mathbf{M}\,\mathbf{y}(x_L),
\qquad
\mathbf{M} = \prod_n \mathbf{M}_n,
$$

where each $\mathbf{M}_n$ is the local RK4 step operator.

## Asymptotic Boundary Conditions

Outside the region where $V(x)$ is appreciable, the potential is assumed to approach constant asymptotic values, so the solutions become plane waves with wavenumbers

$$
k_{L} = \sqrt{\tfrac{2m}{\hbar^2}(E - V_{-\infty})}, \qquad
k_{R} = \sqrt{\tfrac{2m}{\hbar^2}(E - V_{+\infty})}.
$$

For a wave incident from the left, the physically appropriate asymptotic forms are

$$
\psi(x) \sim
\begin{cases}
e^{ik_L x} + r\,e^{-ik_L x}, & x \to -\infty, \\[4pt]
t\,e^{ik_R x}, & x \to +\infty,
\end{cases}
$$

where $r$ and $t$ are the reflection and transmission amplitudes. The corresponding derivative $\phi = \psi'$ follows directly.

## Extraction of Scattering Amplitudes

Imposing a purely outgoing wave on the right boundary,

$$
\mathbf{y}(x_R) =
t
\begin{pmatrix} 1 \\ i k_R \end{pmatrix}
e^{ik_R x_R},
$$

and expressing the left boundary in terms of incident and reflected components,

$$
\mathbf{y}(x_L) =
\begin{pmatrix} e^{ik_L x_L} + r\,e^{-ik_L x_L} \\
i k_L\!\left(e^{ik_L x_L} - r\,e^{-ik_L x_L}\right)
\end{pmatrix},
$$

substitution into $\mathbf{y}(x_R) = \mathbf{M}\,\mathbf{y}(x_L)$ produces two linear algebraic equations in the two unknowns $r$ and $t$. Denoting the transfer matrix elements by $M_{ij}$, one solves this $2\times 2$ system to obtain closed-form expressions. Written compactly in terms of the boundary vectors, the amplitudes are

$$
r = \frac{
(M_{11} + i k_R^{-1} M_{21}\cdot i k_R)\cdots
}{\Delta},
\qquad
t = \frac{\text{(incident determinant)}}{\Delta},
$$

where $\Delta$ is the determinant of the coefficient matrix formed from the columns representing the reflected and transmitted plane waves. In practice these are evaluated numerically from the propagated $\mathbf{M}$.

## Reflection and Transmission Coefficients

The observable coefficients are constructed from the probability current,

$$
R = |r|^2, \qquad
T = \frac{k_R}{k_L}\,|t|^2.
$$

For a real potential, unitarity guarantees $R + T = 1$. For a complex potential, the non-Hermiticity of the Hamiltonian implies

$$
R + T = 1 - A,
$$

where $A$ quantifies net absorption ($A>0$) or amplification ($A<0$). This deficit is a direct signature of the imaginary part $V_I(x)$ and is faithfully reproduced by the RK-propagated transfer matrix, provided the step size $h$ is chosen small enough to resolve the shortest oscillation length $2\pi/\mathrm{Re}[k(x)]$ and the attenuation scale set by $\mathrm{Im}[k(x)]$.

## Concluding Remarks

The Runge-Kutta approach thus reduces the scattering problem for an arbitrary complex potential to (i) the numerical construction of a transfer matrix by high-order integration of the coupled first-order system, and (ii) the algebraic matching of this matrix to asymptotic plane-wave boundary conditions. The resulting formulae for $r$, $t$, $R$, and $T$ are exact in the limit of vanishing step size and provide a robust, flexible framework for studying absorption, resonance, and non-Hermitian scattering phenomena that lack analytic solutions.

# Abstract

**One-Dimensional Scattering from Complex PT-Symmetric Potentials: A Numerical Investigation of Unidirectional Invisibility and Spectral Singularities**

We present a systematic study of quantum scattering in one dimension governed by complex potentials satisfying parity-time (PT) symmetry, characterized by the condition V(x) = V*(−x). While non-Hermitian, such potentials admit real energy eigenvalues within an unbroken symmetry regime, motivating their relevance to both quantum mechanics and optical wave propagation in media with balanced gain and loss. This work examines the scattering signatures unique to PT-symmetric systems, with emphasis on unidirectional invisibility, anomalous transmission and reflection asymmetries, and the emergence of spectral singularities corresponding to divergent scattering amplitudes.

The principal innovation of this study lies in the unified treatment of transfer-matrix formalism adapted to non-Hermitian scattering, enabling direct identification of the parameter regimes where left- and right-incident reflection coefficients decouple. We demonstrate that the generalized unitarity relation, |T − 1|² = |R_L R_R|, replaces the conventional probability conservation law and provides a rigorous framework for classifying scattering behavior across the symmetry-breaking threshold.

Numerically, we employ a piecewise-constant discretization of the potential combined with cascaded transfer-matrix multiplication, cross-validated against direct integration of the stationary Schrödinger equation via a fourth-order Runge–Kutta scheme. This dual approach ensures numerical stability in regimes where reflection amplitudes grow unbounded near spectral singularities. Results confirm the predicted asymmetry between reflectionless directions and reveal a continuous evolution from invisibility to amplification as the non-Hermiticity parameter increases.

These findings clarify the interplay between PT symmetry, reciprocity, and conservation laws in open scattering systems, offering quantitative benchmarks for the design of optical devices exploiting gain-loss engineering.

*Keywords:* PT symmetry, non-Hermitian scattering, transfer matrix, spectral singularity, unidirectional invisibility
